Because the same mechanism gives you three things ML platforms constantly rebuild by hand: continuously updated feature tables, changelog streams that feed incremental training or online learning jobs, and point-in-time training snapshots you can reproduce later. This post is a source tour of the apache/paimon repository on the master branch — every class and line number below was verified against the actual tree, and the two diagrams were generated from the code layout.

The overview path: engines connect through a catalog to a FileStoreTable, which anchors a metadata tree of snapshots and manifests on top of an LSM data layout, while consumers track their position in the stream.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Engines land as sinks and catalogs. Flink writes through the abstract FlinkSink, L76, and Spark mounts tables through SparkCatalog, L128. If you already run Flink, the sink integrates with its checkpoint exactly-once machinery.
  • The catalog is the front door. Everything resolves through the Catalog, L61 interface, which turns database and table names into table objects backed by real files.
  • One table abstraction, two behaviors. FileStoreTable, L59 extends DataTable; primary-key tables and append tables share it, differing only in the store and merge behavior behind them.
  • Snapshots are the consistency unit. Each commit produces a Snapshot, L44 — an immutable pointer to a manifest list. Readers pick a snapshot and see a frozen table version.
  • Snapshot discovery is its own class. SnapshotManager, L201 resolves the latest snapshot, tolerating concurrent commits, and enumerates history for time travel.
  • Manifests describe the file set. A snapshot references a ManifestList, L46, whose manifest files carry add/delete entries for every data file — the same idea Iceberg popularized.
  • Primary-key tables run an LSM. KeyValueFileStore, L56 organizes data as SST files in levels, merged by configurable merge engines.
  • Compaction keeps reads cheap. MergeTreeCompactManager, L54 picks overlapping sorted runs and rewrites them into fewer, larger files in the background.
  • Consumers pin the stream. ConsumerManager, L44 persists named positions so a downstream job can resume from the exact snapshot it last processed.

The detail view adds the commit protocol, branches and tags, the merge-function family, index files, deletion vectors, and snapshot expiration.

Why a Streaming Lakehouse Table Matters for AI

A feature table in Paimon behaves like a changelog with a queryable present tense. When you write an upsert, the table produces both a new data file and — depending on configuration — a changelog record. The ChangelogProducer enum in CoreOptions (line 5439) defines the modes: from none up to lookup and full-compaction, trading write cost against downstream completeness. A Flink job can consume that changelog to keep an online feature store warm while Spark training jobs scan the same table as a batch source. One copy of the data, two consumption models, no nightly export glue.

The snapshot mechanism is equally important for ML. Training runs that must be reproducible can read a tagged snapshot instead of whatever happens to be in the table today. Tags extend snapshots (Tag, L44 literally extends Snapshot), and BranchManager, L31 gives you isolated branches of a table — handy for testing a schema change or backfilling features without disturbing production consumers.

Snapshots, Manifests, and the Commit Protocol

Every write ends in the same place: FileStoreCommitImpl, the class at L146 that publishes the next snapshot. It carries a commitUser identifier (line 154) and runs an optimistic tryCommit loop (line 974): attempt to swap the manifest list, and on conflict re-read, re-merge manifest entries, and retry. This is how dozens of concurrent Flink writer subtasks — or independent Spark jobs — commit to one table without a central lock server.

The metadata tree is deliberately file-based. A snapshot file names its manifest list; the manifest list names manifests; each ManifestFile, L57 holds ManifestEntry records (line 42) describing one data file each. Scans prune partitions and buckets from these small metadata files before ever touching data. Iceberg readers will recognize the shape immediately — the Paimon README explicitly credits Iceberg’s design, and the repo even ships an Iceberg compatibility module.

Inside the LSM Tree: Levels and Merge Engines

The write path for a primary-key table is KeyValueFileStoreWrite, L72, which manages one merge tree per bucket. Records buffer in MergeTreeWriter, L60, get flushed as sorted runs into Levels, L39, and the compact manager merges runs whose key ranges overlap. Each data file is described by a DataFileMeta (line 61): level, key range, statistics.

What makes this interesting for feature engineering is the merge-engine pluggability. MergeFunctionFactory, L29 manufactures the function that folds same-key records: deduplicate keeps the newest, PartialUpdateMergeFunction, L67 merges non-null fields across rows — ideal when different jobs own different feature columns — and FirstRowMergeFunction, L32 keeps only the first record per key, a cheap dedup for click streams. The MergeEngine enum in CoreOptions (line 5264) exposes these as a table property.

Deletion vectors round out the mutation story. BucketedDvMaintainer, L35 tracks which rows are deleted per bucket, and DeletionVectorsIndexFile, L44 persists that index so reads can hide rows without immediate rewrites — merge-on-read deletes with merge-on-write options available.

Bucketing and the Append-Table Path

Before any record reaches an LSM tree, Paimon decides which bucket it belongs to. Bucketing is the table’s unit of parallelism: each bucket gets its own writer, its own sorted runs, and its own compaction schedule, so a sensible bucket count keeps Flink writer subtasks evenly loaded. For dynamic-bucket primary-key tables, the HashIndexFile, L32 persists the mapping from primary key to bucket, letting later writes find an existing key’s home without a full scan; the BucketAssigner, L24 interface abstracts that decision, and a cross-partition variant in the crosspartition package handles keys that move between partitions.

Append tables skip all of this machinery. AppendOnlyFileStore, L45 simply writes immutable files — no merge functions, no levels — which makes it the cheapest possible ingestion path for telemetry, event logs, and raw training corpora. Auto-compaction can still merge many small files into fewer large ones in the background, and deletion vectors can even be enabled on append tables for simple deduplication. For AI workloads that mostly append feature rows and occasionally rewrite history, the append variant is often the right default, while the primary-key LSM earns its cost when entities genuinely get updated in place.

From Install to Your First Model

Here the honest path, straight from the repository README. Building from source requires JDK 8 or 11 and Maven 3.6.3 or newer; then run:

mvn clean install -DskipTests

(Contributors also run mvn spotless:apply to keep formatting clean.) That produces the engine JARs you register: the Flink connector for streaming jobs, the Spark connector for SQL analytics. Point a Flink or Spark session’s catalog at your object storage path — the Catalog implementations handle file layout, including the filesystem and REST catalog variants — and declare your first primary-key table with a CREATE TABLE statement in the engine’s SQL dialect, marking the key PRIMARY KEY NOT ENFORCED and choosing a merge engine and changelog producer as table options.

From there your “model” is a discipline rather than a command: start a streaming job writing upserts into the feature table, set a changelog mode your consumers can honor, and let downstream jobs read the same table. The full engine-by-engine quickstarts, DDL examples, and configuration tables live in the official documentation at paimon.apache.org, which the README names as the canonical entry point — worth following rather than paraphrasing, because option defaults move with releases.

Honest Limits

The README makes no performance claims, and neither should a blog post. The repository contains a benchmark module, but no published numbers you can copy into an architecture decision, so benchmark Paimon against your own workload before committing to it. Second, primary-key tables buy merge-on-read convenience with real costs: compaction consumes background resources, and read latency depends on how many sorted runs a key spans — append tables avoid this but give up upserts. Third, changelog completeness is a spectrum: the cheap modes can produce changelogs only at compaction points, so exactly-once downstream semantics need the pricier modes or careful planning. Fourth, snapshot accumulation is your operational responsibility — ExpireSnapshotsImpl, L64 implements expiration behind the ExpireSnapshots interface, but you must schedule it, respecting pinned consumers. Finally, Paimon is JVM-first: the connectors target Flink and Spark runtimes, and building the project itself pins JDK 8/11, so teams that live purely in Python will still operate some Java.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of Apache Paimon: snapshots, manifests, LSM merge engines, and how streaming updates become batch-readable tables for continuously fresh AI feature data.

entry.title: Presto Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Distributed SQL Engine That Queries Your Whole Lakehouse

link.title: Presto Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Distributed SQL Engine That Queries Your Whole Lakehouse

entry.content:
Presto describes itself in one line in its own README: “Presto is a distributed SQL query engine for big data.” That modest sentence hides one of the most influential architectures in data infrastructure. Born at Facebook to let engineers query petabyte Hive warehouses interactively, Presto evolved into a federation engine: one SQL surface in front of Hive, Iceberg, Delta Lake, Kafka, MySQL, PostgreSQL, Elasticsearch and dozens of other systems, each reached through a clean connector interface. Where Spark’s SQL engine is fused to Spark’s compute model, Presto treats query execution and data access as separate concerns, which is exactly why it spread across the industry and inspired siblings like Trino.

If you work on AI or ML systems, Presto matters to you even if you have never typed its name. Training data rarely lives in one place: features sit in lakehouse tables, labels arrive from event streams like Kafka topics, embeddings and model artifacts rest in object stores such as MinIO, and dashboards over experiment results query the same cluster. Presto is the layer that answers “join this parquet lake with that Postgres feature table and give me a training set” without anyone first copying data into yet another store. It is not a model trainer or a GPU runtime; it is the query muscle that turns scattered artifacts into tabular data ready for PyTorch, scikit-learn or a DuckDB laptop session.

This post is a source tour, not a marketing page. We cloned prestodb/presto at commit e0939e3 on the master branch, read the coordinator and worker code paths, and drew two architecture diagrams from what is actually in the repository today. Every code link below points at a real file and line on master.

The end-to-end data path: a SQL statement arrives over HTTP, is parsed, analyzed, planned and fragmented on the coordinator, then executed as stages of tasks on workers, each reading through the connector SPI.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • A client submits SQL through QueuedStatementResource.postStatement, L213, the JAX-RS endpoint behind POST /v1/statement; results later flow back through ExecutingStatementResource, L99.
  • On the coordinator, DispatchManager.createQuery, L234 mints a query ID, enqueues the statement into a resource group and hands it off for dispatch.
  • Semantic resolution happens in Analyzer.analyzeSemantic, L111, which walks the AST, checks types and enforces access control before any data moves.
  • The optimized relational plan is produced by LogicalPlanner.plan, L185 and its rule-based optimizer chain.
  • PlanFragmenter.createSubPlans, L74 then cuts that plan into stage fragments at exchange boundaries — the unit of distributed work.
  • The per-query orchestrator SqlQueryExecution.start, L491 ties it all together and kicks off SqlQueryScheduler.createSqlQueryScheduler, L158.
  • Splits — the per-task chunks of table data — come from SplitManager.getSplits, L73, which delegates into the connector.
  • On workers, ConnectorPageSourceProvider.createPageSource, L32 opens the actual data stream, and ExchangeClient, L71 shuttles serialized pages between stages over HTTP.

Now let us zoom into the internals.

The detailed view: eight subsystems from server bootstrap to connector SPI, with the coordinator-side planning stack on one side and worker-side task execution on the other.

From Install to Your First Model

The README keeps the requirements tight: Mac OS X or Linux, 64-bit Java 17, Maven 3.6.3+ for building, and Python 2.4+ only for the launcher script. Building the engine from the project root is a single Maven command:

./mvnw clean install -DskipTests

The README warns honestly that the first build downloads all dependencies into your local ~/.m2/repository and takes a considerable amount of time; later builds are faster. Once it finishes, you can run a coordinator straight from IntelliJ with main class com.facebook.presto.server.PrestoServer, the presto-main classpath module, and VM options that point at the sample config: -ea -XX:+UseG1GC -Xmx2G -Dconfig=etc/config.properties -Dlog.levels-file=etc/log.properties. The Hive plugin expects a metastore address such as -Dhive.metastore.uri=thrift://localhost:9083, which you can drop if you have none yet.

Start the CLI from presto-cli/target/presto-cli-*-executable.jar and confirm the cluster sees itself:

SELECT * FROM system.runtime.nodes;

In the sample configuration the Hive connector is mounted as the hive catalog, so SHOW TABLES FROM hive.default; lists whatever the metastore exposes. For the ML use case, this is the moment it clicks: point a Hive, Iceberg or Delta catalog at your lakehouse, CREATE TABLE AS SELECT your engineered features from wherever they live, and the output table is immediately queryable as a training-set source. If you would rather provision the cluster on containers, a Kubernetes deployment pairs well with object storage in the same cluster.

Inside the Coordinator

Bootstrap starts at PrestoServer.run, L122, which assembles a large Guice module graph and then loads catalogs, function namespaces, access control and event listeners before logging SERVER STARTED. The server is deliberately a composition root: almost everything interesting — DiscoveryNodeManager, L88 for cluster membership, CatalogManager, L29 for mounted connectors — arrives as injected services.

Query lifecycle state is centralized in QueryStateMachine.begin, L225, which walks an explicit state machine — QueryState, L25 enumerates QUEUED, PLANNING, STARTING, RUNNING, FINISHING, FINISHED and FAILED — with timed transitions like transitionToRunning, L851. That explicit machine is what makes the web UI and the system.runtime.queries table trustworthy: they read the same source of truth.

Even the path into the engine is layered. Statement text is parsed by SqlParser.createStatement, L100 inside the standalone presto-parser module, an ANTLR-based grammar with no runtime coupling to the rest of the server — which is why other tools can reuse it to parse Presto-dialect SQL. Submission and waiting are explicit too: DispatchManager.waitForDispatched, L362 lets the protocol layer block until the coordinator has actually handed the query to the execution machinery, giving the client a clean QUEUED-to-RUNNING progression instead of a race against internal state.

Protection against runaway queries is not bolted on. SqlQueryManager.createQuery, L304 registers each execution in a tracker, and a scheduled enforcement loop checks memory, CPU time, scan bytes, output size and written-intermediate limits every second. For a shared analytics cluster serving both BI dashboards and ad-hoc feature queries, that guardrail layer is the difference between a useful service and a weekend pager.

How Splits Become Pages

The distributed execution model rests on three vocabulary words: stages, splits and pages. A fragment from the PlanFragmenter becomes a stage; a stage is instantiated as tasks on many nodes; each task processes splits. NodeScheduler.selectDistributionNodes, L406 decides which node gets which split, balancing load against data locality, while the StageScheduler.schedule, L28 interface lets the engine swap in different placement strategies.

Delivery of work happens over HTTP: HttpRemoteTaskFactory.createRemoteTask, L234 packages a plan fragment plus its split assignments and pushes it to the chosen worker. On the worker, LocalExecutionPlanner.plan, L493 compiles the fragment into local drivers of operators, and data itself moves as columnar pages — batches of typed vectors, not row objects. Between stages, ExchangeClient, L71 pulls SerializedPage batches from upstream task output buffers through the PageBufferClient. This page-exchange design is why Presto can stream results instead of materializing intermediate tables on disk.

Worker-side bookkeeping is centralized in SqlTaskManager, L100, which owns every task the node is executing and reports status back to the coordinator. Tasks are also the unit of backpressure: when a downstream exchange buffer fills, upstream tasks slow their production rather than spill unboundedly, which keeps large shuffles — the join fan-out behind a big feature-building query, say — predictable instead of explosive.

The Connector SPI: One Interface, Many Lakes

The reason Presto can front dozens of systems is a deliberately small SPI. ConnectorFactory.create, L32 instantiates one Connector per catalog name; ConnectorMetadata, L77 exposes schemas, tables, statistics and writes; ConnectorSplitManager.getSplits, L30 enumerates the physical chunks; and ConnectorPageSourceProvider.createPageSource, L32 turns a split into a stream of pages. Splits arrive asynchronously via ConnectorSplitSource.getNextBatch, L27, so slow metadata lookups never block the scheduler.

For AI teams this interface is the strategic part of the codebase. A feature store backed by MySQL, a parquet lake under Iceberg, and an event log in Kafka are all “just catalogs” — queryable in one statement with joins across them, no export scripts involved. Every call into a connector carries a ConnectorSession, L31, the SPI handle for user identity, timezone and catalog-specific session properties, so the same statement can behave differently per catalog without special cases in the engine. Memory governance wraps all of it: ClusterMemoryManager, L106 watches cluster-wide usage and assigns queries to bounded pools like MemoryPool, L45, so one exploratory 200 GB join cannot starve the feature-refresh queries that feed nightly training.

Honest Limits

Presto’s own README sets expectations correctly, and so should you. The build is heavyweight: the first ./mvnw clean install pulls the entire dependency tree, and the README notes the test suite takes several minutes even before you reach distributed integration tests. The supported host list is explicit — Mac OS X or Linux — so a native Windows dev box means WSL or containers. The sample configuration leans on a Hive metastore; without one you will be hand-editing catalog properties to get a first query through.

Architecturally, the same federation strength carries a cost. Every connector has its own capabilities: predicate pushdown, statistics and transactional writes vary widely across catalogs, so plans that look identical on two systems can perform very differently. Presto is a query engine, not a training platform — it will not gradient-descent anything, and it is the wrong tool for millisecond lookup serving, which is what caches like Redis are for. For strict wire compatibility with the Trino dialect you will encounter ecosystem differences, as the community fork shows. And for raw compute-heavy scans, the README points to Presto native, a C++ worker rewrite built on Meta’s Velox engine — a separate execution story living in the same repository. None of these limits are hidden; they are just real.
entry.summary: A guided tour through the prestodb/presto source tree: how a SQL statement becomes stages, splits and pages, and why Presto is the federation layer for AI and ML data.

entry.title: Inside Apache Spark: How One Line of SQL Becomes a Cluster Job

link.title: Inside Apache Spark: How One Line of SQL Becomes a Cluster Job

entry.content:
The best description of this project is the one its authors wrote: the README's first line calls Apache Spark "a unified analytics engine for large-scale data processing." That phrasing undersells what the repository actually holds. Behind that sentence sits a SQL parser, a rule-based and cost-aware query optimizer, a whole-stage code generator, a distributed DAG scheduler, a shuffle machinery, a unified memory manager, and a micro-batch streaming engine — all in Scala, all on the JVM. On top of the core, the same README lists Spark SQL for SQL and DataFrames, a pandas API on Spark for pandas workloads, MLlib for machine learning, GraphX for graph processing, and Structured Streaming for stream processing. One process model, one scheduler, one memory manager, stretched from a laptop to thousands of nodes.

For anyone building AI systems, Spark is the tool you reach for the moment a dataset stops fitting on the machine that runs your notebook. Feature engineering over billions of rows, tokenizing a raw crawl before a training run, deduplicating text before it lands in a vector store, joining click logs with labels to assemble shuffled training batches — these are exactly the "too big for a single process" jobs that single-node engines like Polars and Python-native ones like Dask attack from other directions. Spark attacks the same problem from the JVM side: the engine keeps planning on a driver process, ships serialized tasks to executors, and treats everything — batch SQL, ML training data prep, streaming windows — as DAGs of stages.

The repository rewards reading it. The path from one line of SQL to tasks running on worker nodes crosses a handful of clearly named subsystems, and every one of them is greppable in the tree. The two diagrams in this post were generated directly from the master branch of apache/spark, and every link in the walkthrough below points at a real file and line number you can open on GitHub.

The overview path: the DataFrame and SQL API builds logical plans, Catalyst analyzes and optimizes them, physical planning produces a code-generated plan, and the DAGScheduler turns lineage into stages and tasks that run on executors — with the micro-batch streaming engine feeding the same core.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • SparkSession, L63 is the entry point every session starts from; its def sql, L538 turns SQL text into a DataFrame.
  • Dataset, L125 carries an unresolved logical plan; each select, L1195 or filter just wraps it in another node.
  • QueryExecution, L67 is the state machine of one query: analyzed, L238, optimizedPlan, L361, and finally executedPlan, L404.
  • Analyzer batches, L674 resolve names, functions, and types against the catalog.
  • Optimizer batches, L564 rewrite the resolved plan at fixed point until nothing changes.
  • AdaptiveSparkPlanExec, L71 re-plans the physical plan between shuffle stages using runtime statistics.
  • SparkContext.runJob, L2858 is where a finished plan becomes a job on the cluster.
  • DAGScheduler.runJob, L1886 splits RDD lineage into stages and submitMissingTasks, L3215 ships them out.
  • Executor.launchTask, L551 deserializes each task on a worker and runs it against its partition.

The internals view: Catalyst rule batches, physical strategies, code generation, stage splitting into result and shuffle-map tasks, executor-side storage and memory, and the DStream graph that JobGenerator ticks once per batch interval.

Inside the Optimizer

Catalyst is the reason you can write sloppy SQL and still get fast jobs. The Analyzer, L404 first walks your unresolved plan with fixed-point Resolution batches, L674, binding table names through the catalog and inferring types along the way. The Optimizer, L51 then applies its rule batches, L564 repeatedly — predicate pushdown, column pruning, constant folding, join reordering — until the plan stops changing, and a Finish Analysis batch, L186 cleans up the rest. Only then does JoinSelection, L200 decide, per join, between broadcast, shuffle-hash, and sort-merge execution; large joins typically land in SortMergeJoinExec, L39.

The JVM payoff is WholeStageCodegenExec, L744: whole chains of operators get fused into a single generated Java function, produced by doCodeGen, L780, so a filter and an aggregation over the same rows become one tight loop with no virtual-call overhead between them. The boundaries where fusion cannot happen are the ShuffleExchangeExec, L190 nodes — and those are precisely where AdaptiveSparkPlanExec, L71 waits to re-plan once it can count the actual shuffle output.

Scheduling, Shuffle, and Memory

Below the SQL layer everything is RDDs. An RDD, L84 is a partitioned lineage with just enough information to recompute any lost partition. An action calls SparkContext.runJob, L2858, which hands the DAG to the scheduler. handleJobSubmitted, L2619 builds the final stage via createResultStage, L988, walking shuffle dependencies backward; each shuffle boundary produces a map stage created by createShuffleMapStage, L737. Two task types do the work: ShuffleMapTask, L54 writes its partition's output for the next stage, and ResultTask, L55 returns the final answer to the driver.

Placement is the resourceOffers, L573 loop in TaskSchedulerImpl, L83, which matches pending tasks to the cores that executors have offered. On the worker side, Executor.launchTask, L551 runs each task on a thread pool thread. Shuffle files and cached partitions both flow through the BlockManager, L183, while UnifiedMemoryManager, L58 splits the heap between execution and storage pools and lets them borrow from each other — which is why caching a big dataset and running an aggregation rarely deadlock each other's memory.

Streaming the Micro-batch Way

The streaming/ module is the classic DStream engine, and it is a masterclass in reusing a batch system. A DStream, L64 is just a sequence of RDDs, one per interval. StreamingContext.start, L581 activates the scheduler, and a timer in JobGenerator.generateJobs, L251 walks the DStream graph every interval; terminal nodes like ForEachDStream.generateJob, L47 produce an ordinary Spark job, which JobScheduler.submitJobSet, L145 hands to the same DAGScheduler the batch engine uses. The result: your stream processing literally becomes tiny batch jobs on a clock, with fault tolerance borrowed from RDD recomputation.

Worth knowing when you read modern docs: the README names Structured Streaming as the stream-processing story, treating the stream as an unbounded table over the SQL engine, while the DStream engine diagrammed above remains in the tree as the older micro-batch machinery. Same clock idea, different API layer — and the diagrams in this post map the machinery that both of them eventually land on.

From Install to Your First Model

The fastest path, straight from the README: download a prebuilt package from spark.apache.org (no build needed), then start the Scala shell with ./bin/spark-shell. The README's own smoke test is spark.range(1000 * 1000 * 1000).count(), which should print 1,000,000,000 — that single line exercises session creation, planning, stage scheduling, and execution end to end. Python users get the identical flow with ./bin/pyspark and the same one-liner, and it is the natural first cell before pointing a DataFrame at real training data.

Ready-made examples ship in the repo: ./bin/run-example SparkPi runs the Pi estimator locally, and prefixing MASTER=spark://host:7077 points the same command at a standalone cluster (or yarn). If you want to build from source instead, the README specifies ./build/mvn -DskipTests clean package with Apache Maven, and ./dev/run-tests once built. MLlib ships in the same distribution, so once the shell runs, the "first model" is a matter of assembling a DataFrame and letting the engine distribute the rest — no extra cluster software to install for a first run.

Honest Limits

First, the JVM tax. The engine core is Scala and requires a modern JDK to build and run, and the README's build matrix treats Java 21 as the baseline; a source build also couples you to the Hadoop version your cluster runs, because Spark uses the Hadoop core library to talk to HDFS. Second, language drift: the README marks the R API as deprecated, and the connect-based remote sessions show where the project is heading — the classic JVM-embedded session is no longer the only execution mode, but the mature tooling still assumes it. Third, the driver is a real constraint: planning, stage splitting, and task bookkeeping all live in one driver process, so a pathologically wide query plan is a driver-side problem no amount of executors fixes. Fourth, shuffle is materialized — map tasks write files that downstream tasks fetch through the BlockManager, so an unplanned join explosion shows up as disk and network I/O, which is exactly the class of problem AdaptiveSparkPlanExec exists to mitigate at runtime. Finally, micro-batch means latency floors at the batch interval: sub-second streaming is a Structured Streaming and continuous-processing conversation, not a DStream one. None of these limits is a secret — they are all visible in the README or in the source paths cited above, which is exactly why reading the tree pays off before you commit a workload to it.

How It Fits an AI Stack

In a modern ML platform, Spark is the heavy-duty stage between raw storage and anything that trains or serves. It reads from object stores and warehouses, runs the join-and-aggregate grind of feature engineering, and hands off parquet shards or training tables to whatever consumes them. [Kafka](/kafka/) is its natural streaming front door, with the micro-batch engine above picking up where the broker leaves off. For interactive federation over the same lake, [Trino](/trino/) answers the ad-hoc SQL while Spark does the long-running batch; and if your data comfortably fits one machine, the honest comparison points are [Polars](/polars/) and [Dask](/dask/) before you reach for a cluster. The source tree teaches the shape of every large-scale engine that came after it — plan, optimize, schedule, shuffle — which is why it remains worth an afternoon of reading.
